Project under review: /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management (a RISC-V bare-metal OS lab, SV39 paging, 2 harts, global kernel lock).
The newly written code is in kernel/mm/mm.c, kernel/sched/sched.c and include/os/mm.h (see `cd /workspace && git diff`).
Everything else in the tree is given/unmodifiable context: init/main.c, arch/riscv/kernel/{entry.S,boot.c,start.S}, arch/riscv/include/pgtable.h, include/os/{sched.h,elf.h,mm.h}, kernel/irq/irq.c, kernel/syscall/syscall.c, drivers/screen.c, test/*.c, tiny_libc/.
Key facts you must verify against the real files rather than assume:
- user ELFs link at 0x10000 but their PT_LOAD segment starts at vaddr 0xf000 (headers included), memsz up to ~0x3e98.
- USER_STACK_ADDR = 0xf00010000, PGDIR_PA = 0x5e000000, kernel window VPN2 = 0x101, KERNEL_MEM_OFFSET = 0xffffffc000000000.
- main.c init_pcb() loads the shell with load_elf(..., get_kva_of) which only WALKS the page table, so init_page_table() must pre-map the code pages.
- main.c's idle loop frees each exited task's kernel stack with free_user_page(kva2pa(kernel_stack_base - PAGE_SIZE)).
- there is no satp switch in entry.S, so scheduler() must do it.
Only report defects in the NEW code. Do not report pre-existing issues in given files unless the new code depends on them incorrectly.

A reviewer claims the following defect in the NEW code. Try hard to REFUTE it by reading the actual files. Default to refuted=true when you cannot demonstrate a concrete failure.

TITLE: init_user_stack can write past the single user stack frame into the physically preceding frame
FILE: /workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c
CLAIM: init_user_stack() maps exactly one page (line 138) and then copies argv into it with no check that `sp` stays >= top_va - PAGE_SIZE. The only limit is MAX_EXEC_ARGC = 16 entries; individual string lengths come from strlen() on caller-controlled pointers and are unbounded. The page holds at most 4096 - 8*(argc+1) bytes of strings (3960 for argc=16).

Failure scenario: `sys_exec("rw", 16, argv, ...)` with 16 arguments of ~300 bytes each (4800 bytes). At line 157-158 `sp` walks below 0xf0000f000, so STACK_KVA(sp) walks below the frame base and memcpy writes ~840 bytes into the *physically preceding* frame through the kernel direct map (pa2kva). That frame is an unrelated live process's page - silent cross-process corruption with no fault, since the kernel window maps all of 0x50000000-0x60000000 R/W. If the stack frame handed out happens to be the first user frame (pa 0x51000000 == USER_MEM_BEGIN), the overflow lands at 0x50fff000, inside the kernel heap region (KERNEL_MEM_BEGIN..KERNEL_MEM_END).

This is also reachable indirectly from the shipped shell: test_shell.c prints "Too many arguments!" but keeps parsing, so with 11+ words `sys_exec(argv[1], 10, _argv, ...)` is issued while `_argv` only has MAX_ARGC-1 = 9 entries; init_user_stack reads _argv[9]/_argv[10] off the end of the shell's frame and strlen()s whatever garbage pointer it finds, which can yield a length far larger than a page. The kernel must clamp the total to the frame it allocated regardless of what the caller passes.

content.text:
I read the actual sources and could not refute this — the claim holds up in every detail I checked.

**Code (`/workspace/Project4-Virtual_Memory_Management/kernel/sched/sched.c`, lines 135-177)**

```c
uintptr_t top_kva = alloc_page_helper(top_va - PAGE_SIZE, (uintptr_t)new_pcb->pgdir) + PAGE_SIZE;
#define STACK_KVA(va) (top_kva - (top_va - (uintptr_t)(va)))
...
if (argc > MAX_EXEC_ARGC) argc = MAX_EXEC_ARGC;   /* only argc is clamped */
for (i = argc - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    int len = strlen(argv[i]) + 1;                /* unbounded, user-controlled */
    sp -= len;
    memcpy((uint8_t *)STACK_KVA(sp), ..., len);   /* no sp >= top_va - PAGE_SIZE check */
}
```

Facts verified against the tree, not assumed:

- `alloc_page_helper` (mm.c:213-239) returns `pa2kva(get_pa(*pte))` — the kva of exactly **one** frame, so `top_kva` is the frame's end in the direct map and `STACK_KVA(sp)` below `top_va - PAGE_SIZE` addresses the *physically preceding* frame. Confirmed by `pa2kva` = `pa + 0xffffffc000000000` (pgtable.h:139).
- The write cannot fault: `map_kernel_page` (arch/riscv/kernel/boot.c:35-44) installs 128 × 2MB leaf entries covering pa `0x50000000-0x60000000` with `_PAGE_READ|_PAGE_WRITE|_PAGE_EXEC|ACCESSED|DIRTY`. Frames start at `USER_MEM_BEGIN = 0x51000000`, so an overflow of up to ~16MB stays inside mapped, writable kernel window — silent corruption, no trap.
- The data is fully user-controlled: `handle_syscall` (kernel/syscall/syscall.c:9-13) passes `regs[10..13]` straight to `syscall[SYSCALL_EXEC] = do_exec` (init/main.c:131); `do_exec` (sched.c:185-249) does `enable_sum()` and hands `argc`/`argv` to `init_user_stack` with no copy-in, no per-string length limit, and no total-size limit. `strlen` (libs/string.c:21) is an unbounded scan.
- The clamp that *is* present (`argc <= MAX_EXEC_ARGC = 16`, and `string_va[16]` is correctly sized) shows the author bounded the count but not the bytes.

Consequences, refined against the real allocator (first-fit over `user_page[]`, mm.c:50-77):

- `init_page_table` (mm.c:247-266) allocates 5 code frames (`0xf000..0x14000`) and then the stack frame, so on a non-fragmented free list the frames immediately *below* the stack frame are the new process's **own freshly loaded ELF text** (PT_LOAD `0xf000`, memsz ~0x3e98 → `0xf000..0x12e98`). An overflow past ~4KB clobbers the text that `load_elf` just wrote at sched.c:244 — the process then executes garbage.
- With a fragmented free list (any earlier process exited and `free_user_page`'d its frames), the preceding frame belongs to an unrelated live process, exactly the cross-process corruption described. The `0x50fff000` / kernel-heap variant is the least likely case, since frame 0 (`0x51000000`) is held by the shell's `0xf000` code page for the system's lifetime — but that was stated as a conditional in the claim, not the main scenario.
- Arithmetic checks out: usable string space is `4096 - 8*(argc+1)` = 3960 for argc=16; 16 × 300 = 4800 bytes of strings plus the 136-byte argv array puts `sp` ~840 bytes below the frame base. A hostile/buggy program can do far worse (16 pointers to 4KB buffers → 64KB, ~15 frames).
- Secondary path is also real: `test/test_shell.c:246-275` builds `char *_argv[MAX_ARGC - 1]` (9 entries) but calls `sys_exec(argv[1], argc - 1, _argv, ...)` after only *printing* "Too many arguments!"; with 11+ typed words the kernel reads `_argv[9]`, `_argv[10]` past the shell's array and `strlen`s whatever pointer it finds. Note `handle_page_fault` (mm.c:395-407) maps any user-half address on demand, so a bogus pointer does not even trap — it silently gets a zero page. That path's string bytes are small (the shell's input line is capped at ~54 chars by `print_location_x < SHELL_COMMAND_END`), so it is the weaker of the two triggers; the direct `sys_exec` path is the decisive one.

Fix direction: clamp each `len` and the running `sp` to `top_va - PAGE_SIZE` (drop or truncate arguments that no longer fit), and bound the argv array write the same way.

Only argc is clamped (<= MAX_EXEC_ARGC = 16); per-string and total byte length are unbounded and fully user-controlled: handle_syscall (kernel/syscall/syscall.c:9-13) passes a0-a3 straight to do_exec (init/main.c:131), and do_exec (sched.c:185-249) calls enable_sum() and forwards argc/argv with no copy-in or length validation; kernel strlen (libs/string.c:21) is an unbounded scan. STACK_KVA(sp) below the frame base therefore writes into the physically preceding frame through the direct map (pa2kva = pa + 0xffffffc000000000, pgtable.h:139), and it cannot fault: boot.c:35-44 maps pa 0x50000000-0x60000000 with R/W/X/A/D via 128 2MB leaves, so the corruption is silent. The 0x50fff000/kernel-heap variant is unlikely since frame 0 (pa 0x51000000) is permanently held by the shell's 0xf000 code page, but that was stated conditionally. The shell path is also real (test_shell.c:246-275 passes argc-1 up to 11 while _argv has only 9 entries, so the kernel strlen()s out-of-bounds pointers; handle_page_fault at mm.c:395-407 even maps bogus user addresses on demand instead of trapping), though its string volume is capped by the ~54-char input line, making the direct sys_exec path the decisive trigger.
